messages.author: 47e0d105424c0088
messages.subject: Custom Distribution with double indexing
parts:
I need to code two custom distributions for my customer transaction data. 

The probability of customer j on transaction t getting a data variable X  value of x_{jt} is

  prob( x_{jt} ) = p_{j}^{y_{jt}} * (1 - c_{j})^{x_{jt}} * c_{j}^{y_{jt}}

where p_j and c_j are customer level parameters to be estimated and are linked to customer demographics and y_{jt} is  Y data variable value for customer j  on transaction t.

Similarly, for data variable V getting a value of v_j at the customer level

  prob( v_{j} ) = (1 - p_j)^{v_{j}} + (1 - p_j)


I have coded these distributions as:

model {

.....

for (t in 1:T) { // at the transaction level
   increment_log_prob( y[t] * log( p[cust_id[t]]) + x[t] * log1m(c[cust_id[t]] ) + log(c[cust_id[t]] ) );
}

for (j in 1:J) { // at the customer level
 increment_log_prob(log( p[cust_id[j]] * pow( (1 - c[cust_id[j]]), v[j] ) +  (1 - p[cust_id[j]])  ) );
}

}

The sample code runs through but it is slow. I have not seen any examples for coding custom distributions with double indexing and therefore I wanted to confirm if I was doing this right. 
  • Is this the right approach because I do get the message 'Warning (non-fatal): Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) contains a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.  You must call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform' when I run the sample code.
  • I am not sure how this can be vectorized given the T and J loops. 
  • How I can create user defined functions for this custom distributions so that I could simply say x ~ user_defined_distribution() as mentioned on page 167 of the Stan 2.62 manual.
  • How can I predict x_jt and v_j values based on the custom distribution(s) to check the model? The manual is silent about prediction with custom defined distributions (pg. 159). 

Thanks for your help and patience in reading this through. 

Raghu

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Custom Distribution with double indexing
parts:
1. You need to provide your whole model --- there weren't
any sampling statements in what you sent, so no way to diagnose
the warning.

2. There's not a whole lot more opportunity for
vectorization given our available operations. You've already
properly converted to log-scale multiplies and used the
vectorization built into log_sum_exp.

With things like this:

You might try precomputing three vectors:

log_p_cust_id[t]

log1m_c_cust_id[t]

log_c_cust_id[t]

if they get reused. You can even combine the first and last, for

log_p_cust_id_plus_log_c_cust_id[t]

Removing duplicated subexpressions is a huge savings for autodiff.

3. You just need to define x as the first argument to a function
ending in _log, as indicated in the manual. Then all the increments
go on the inside of the function.

4. Prediction works exactly the same way with custom-defined
functions --- you'll just need to write what you need for prediction.

- Bob

> prob(xjt)=pyjtj∗(1−cj)xjt∗cj

I think that may have been garbled in transmission.

I find it easier in mail to use c[j] and p[j] and what not to disambiguate.


> where
>
> • pj and cj are customer level probability parameters (constrained between 0 and 1) to be estimated and are linked to customer demographics through a logit tranformation and
> • yjt is Y data variable value for customer j on transaction t.
> Similarly, the probability for customer j getting a value of vj for data variable V is
>
> prob(vj)=(1−cj)vj+(1−pj)
> .

That doesn't look like it's going to normalize properly. I also don't
see how it relates to what follows, so I'm a bit lost.

> I created custom probability functions for these probabilities using increment_log_prob.
>
> I also tried to create user defined functions for these probabilities but ran into problems possibly because of indexing issues.
>
> For example, for the first distribution, I want to be able to say:
>
> x[t]∼user_defined_log(y[t]∗log(p[custid[t]])+x[t]∗log1m(c[custid[t]])+log(c[custid[t]]))
>

You wouldn't use the "_log" suffix here. See the manual chapter on
defining functions for how to define user-defined probability functions.

> I tried the following code but it did not work.
>
> functions {
> real xdist_log(int x, int y, real p, real c, int cust_id){
> return y * log(p[cust_id]) + x * log1m(c[cust_id]) + log(c[cust_id]);
> }

If x is an array, you need to declare it as such in the function. Same for
the other arguments. See the chapter in the manual on functions.

>
> real vdist_log(int V, real p, real c, int cust_id2){
> return log_sum_exp( log(p[cust_id2]) + V * log1m(c[cust_id2]) , log1m(p[cust_id2]) ) ;

> As seen in the code below, I am using a logit transformation of the customer level p and c probability estimates. Using the following derivative calculation (for p here) to calculate the log absolute derivative of the logit transformation
>
> log∣∣∣ddplogit(p)∣∣∣=log∣∣∣ddplogp1−p∣∣∣=log(1p∗(1−p))=−log(p∗(1−p))=−[log(p)+log(1−p)]=−[log(p)+log1m(p)]
> I am adding the incremental_log_prob for both p and c logit transformations.
>
> increment_log_prob(-( log(p[n]) + log1m(p[n]) ));
> increment_log_prob(-( log(c[n]) + log1m(c[n]) ));

I always get confused when p[] is used for a variable.
If you logit transform a parameter, then isn't it inverse logit
you want to look at? If you declare a parameter as having
lower=0 and upper=0 constraints, we do this all automatically.

> The addition of these two lines of code increase my program compilation time from about 3 mins to approx 3 hours for a dataset of 250 sample observations (using rstanmulticore package). This change seems to be quite drastic. I am hoping that I am doing something wrong to merit this increase (my overall dataset has about 50,000 observations).

I take it you mean sampling, not compilation time. I think you
need to get the model right on a smaller set of simulated data, then run
it on your actual larger data set. You'll find it takes less time in the
end than trying to debug on a big data set.

- Bob
